speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PURCHASES IN CANADA BY BRITISH GOVERNMENT.
subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO MUNITIONS, AND OTHER SUPPLIES-IMPERIAL EXPENDITURES IN CANADA.
speechtext:
In answer to my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) and my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald), who, I believe, raised the question on Saturday, I desire to read to the House a statement which was handed to the press by the Chairman of the Imperial Munitions Board. It is: Ottawa, 21st August 1917. Towards the close of 1916 the capacity for producing munitions in Great Britain had so Increased that the Minister of Munitions advised that it was unnecessary to continue the production of munitions in the United States for British account, except for a few special lines. The production in Canada, however, was continued as before.
The minister has now advised that it is unnecessary to continue production in Canada on the present scale. Tie has directed that certain lines shall be discontinued; that other lines shall be produced in lessened quantities; while some lines are to be continued as at present.
The effect of this will be to stop the production of shells and components at some plants which are now producing sizes no longer required.
In other plants, where shells are made of sizes of which a reduced output only is required, it will mean working during the day only, thus stopping night work. In other plants, however, where sustained production is required, operations will be continued night as well as day.
These changes have been anticipated by several important Arms, who have already resumed, or are planning to resume, their prewar activities in their own lines, while others are engaged in the production or preparation for production, of equipment needed for ships now under construction or to be built during 1918.
For the further information of the House, I may say that the Dominion Government
has advanced to date to the Imperial Munitions Board, for the purchase of munitions in Canada, the sum of $285,000,000. There has also been advanced to the Imperial Munitions Board by the chartered banks of Canada in the same connection the sum of $100,000,000. The Dominion Government, during many months past, has been advancing to the Imperial Treasury, for the purchase of munitions in Canada, the sum of $25,000,000 per month. During July, we advanced $35,000,000; during August we are advancing $35,000,000, and we have arranged to continue the advances of $25,000,000 a month, during September, October, November and December, so that the Dominion Government will continue to make the advances which we have been .making in the past. As I have pointed out, during July and August we increased the amount of our advances by $10,000,000 each month.
I may also say in this connection, as it has a bearing upon the question of the Imperial expenditure in Canada, that the Government arranged in July, in addition to undertaking the programme which I have mentioned, that is to say, of furnishing $35,000,000 in July, $35,000,000 in August and $25,000,000 per .month for the balance of the year, to furnish the sum of $50,000,000 for the purchase of cheese, hay, oats and flour in Canada. I have repeatedly pointed out to the House that the British Government can purchase on this side of the Atlantic only to the extent that they can raise money on this side of the Atlantic. In order to provide the farmers of Canada with an export market for their cheese, we arranged to provide $40,000,000, which is the export value at the prices fixed of the cheese production of Canada, that $40,000,000 to be paid out during July, August, September and October. In addition to that sum, $10,000,000 was supplied for the purchase of hay, oats and flour. The House will thus get an idea of the magnitude of our financial transactions in connection with the purchase of these supplies in Canada.

The House is aware that, so far as concerns our expenditure in Great Britain and upon the continent-, we borrow money from the Imperial Government. The reason for that is obvious. That expenditure has to be paid in starling money or in the currency of France or Belgium. We, therefore, borrow from Great Britain all money necessary for our expenditures in Great Britain and on the continent in respect of our overseas forces. As a set-off to that expenditure, the Imperial Government asks us here to furnish them with credit from which they may purchase munitions, cheese, hay, oats, and 
other products. The Imperial Munitions Board was created by the Imperial Government. It takes its'instructions from the Imperial Government and gives orders to Canadian manufacturers according to instructions which it" receives from the Imperial Government. As to the details of this administration I am not familiar, because, as I have pointed out, it is an Imperial and not a Dominion Government board. The Imperial Government ask us to place the Imperial Munitions Board in funds from month to month to the- amount that I have mentioned. So far as our transactions are concerned, therefore, they are with the Imperial Government which furnish us with money in. Great Britain and. on the continent, we supplying them with money here with which to pay for their commitments for munitions and. other supplies.

speakerposition: stagedirection

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE BABTIE REPORT-DR. BRUCE'S REPLY.
speechtext:
On various occasions some hon. gentlemen have expressed their desire that a memorandum made by Colonel Bruce with respect to matters set forth in a report of the commission of which General Sir William Babtie was chairman, shall be laid upon the Table of the House.
I have given the .matter the best consideration that I could, and I do not think it is a

document which ought to be laid on the table of the House by the Government.
It is not an official report, as Colonel Bruce was not requested or empowered by any competent authority to make the memorandum in question. That fact is further established by the circumstance that, as 1 am informed, he sent a copy of it to some hon. members of this House, which certainly he would not have done if he had believed it to he an official report in the ordinary sense.
There is also the further consideration that he has been seconded to the Royal Army Medical Service, and I am informed that the memorandum which he has prepared deals with the administration of that service. It seems, therefore, that the War Office ought to be consulted before any document of that kind put forward by an officer of the British service should be laid on the table of this House by the Government.	.
I should also like to correct a misapprehension, which, if I understand correctly, has arisen with regard to his opportunity to be heard before the Babtie Commission, of which Sir William BaWtie was chairman, and four very eminent Canadian surgeons, whose names I have already given to the House, were members. The proceedings of the Board show that Colonel Bruce was called as a witness on November 27, 1916, recalled on November 28, and again on the 6th of December, on which date he was twice heard, and also on the 16th of December. A memorandum has been placed in my hands containing an extract from the secretary of the board, in the following words:
"The Board directs me to say that neither General Jones nor Colonel Bruce asked to he allowed to be present throughout the inquiry being made by the Board."

The Baptie Board. My hon. friend (Sir Sam Hughes) also made inquiry in this connection as to what changes and improvements had been made in the administration of the Canadian Army Medical Service. I have a telegram dated August 23, 1917 from Sir George Perley in the following words:
Prime Minister,
Ottawa.
Director Medical Services submits following:
Department is receptive to suggestions irrespective of their source. All suggestions, recommendations are carefully considered, and if deemed advisable are put into effect. Following are some improvements effected in this service since January 1, 1917.
(1)	Systematic routine inspection of Canadians in hospitals in United Kingdom to select cases requiring further treatment in Canada.
(2)	Establishment of a 1,300-bed hospital at Liverpool to assemble patients for Canada and facilitate prompt embarkation. Arrangements made for assembly insane patients for Canada at Mental Hospital near Liverpool for convenient embarkation.
(3)	Provision of hospital ship service from Liverpool to Canada for invalids.
(4)	Hospital accommodation in England has been expanded by over 5,000 primary beds and sufficient convalescent beds to adequately meet Canadian requirements. Arrangements completed for further expansion that will provide sufficient hospital accommodation for all tuber-culose and venereal patients.
(5)	Arrangements made by which War Office provides reliefs for Canadian medicals units in Mediterranean, these units returning for duty in England.
(6)	Greater economy in use of personnel by deciding number requisite for each medical unit and adhering to such limitation.
(7)	Completion of consultant and inspection service on systematic basis. All patients in Canadian hospitals inspected semi-monthly and routine inspections made of Canadians in British hospitals.
(8)	Improved system for controlling movement and prompt evacuation of patients from hospitals.
(9)	While segregation of Canadians in Canadian hospitals is impracticable and inadvisable, arrangements have been made whereby those sent to British hospitals are distributed to hospitals readily accessible to Canadian inspectors and convenient for movement to Canadian hospitals for final disposition.
(10)	Systematic inspection and control of hospital and medical records to ensure completeness and accuracy of same.
(11)	System for strict control of laboratory service.
(12)	Improved system of controlling hospital food supplies to ensure economy.
(13)	Abolition of dual control of Shorncliffe military hospital group by arranging with British authorities to resume their control and administration. The A. D. M. S., Canadians, Folkestone, at request of British authorities, carries out administration of this group and reports direct to British authorities on all matters pertaining thereto.
(14)	Abolition of dual administration of Red Cross Hospital by C.A.M.C. taking entire control.
(15)	Abolition of purchasing bureau for medical supplies and equipment by turning same over to Quartermaster General's branch.
(16)	Establishment of central medical stores where all medical supplies are received and carefully checked for distribution.
(17)	Improved control of expenditures of medical stores and supplies by more strict and systematic checking of indents from units.
(IS) Decentralization of medical boards and improvement of control through careful routine inspections and uniform standardization.
(19)	Improved medical board form for the purpose of meeting provisions of Canadian pension laws.
(20)	Standardization of fitness of soldiers
according to physical grades, with system of control to	provide uniform	classification
throughout service. .

(21)	Improved system of dealing with officer and nursing sister casualties by which convalescence is spent in hospital instead of on leave, thus controlling and shortening period of non-effectiveness.	-
(22)	Adoption of complete and systematic measures for prevention and spread of communicable disease.
(23)	C.A.M.C. Training School reorganized on proper military basis and staffed with personnel trained at front; an improved syllabus of training adopted based on experience gained in present war.
(24)	Fair and definite policy adopted for promotion of officers and other ranks.
(25)	Definite policy for giving officers overseas service which recognizes prior rights of those who have served longest in England; provision for return of officers of experience from overseas to serve in England or Canada.
(26)	More complete co-ordination with services in France and Canada.
(27)	More complete co-ordination, with exchange of all ranks, between Canadian Corps and medical units on lin.es of communications and at base.
(28)	Arrangements for temporary expansion of army medical units at front during time of action by detail of personnel from medical units on lines of communication and at base.
(29)	The majority of these improvements have been noted in monthly progress reports.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CORRECTION BY FINANCE MINISTER OF STATEMENT IN THE REGINA LEADER.
speechtext:
My attention has been called to an editorial in the Regina Morning Leader with reference to the $100,000,000 loan issue recently made by the Dominion Government in the city of New York, which does a great injustice to the Bank of Montreal. In this editorial the following appears:
But while the Finance Minister of Canada himself d id all the hard work in connection with the flotation of this loan, he allowed the Bank of Montreal a commission of I :l per cent, for lending him its assistance. In other words, out of this loan the Bank of Montreal receives the neat little sum of $1,750,000 as a commission. The commission originally arranged was 2 per cent., hut the Bank of Montreal remitted one-quarter of one per cent., or $250,000.
Why, asks the Toronto Star, and the Leader repeats the question, as we believe the people of Canada will repeat it, should the Bank of Montreal receive nearly two million dollars for its assistance to the minister, who himself negotiated the loan? Why should anybody make nearly two million dollars out of a loan negotiated for a patriotic purpose?
I desire to explain to the House, although so far as the House is concerned I believe the explanation is unnecessary, that the Bank of Montreal being our fiscal agents, the general manager, Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor, usually negotiates our foreign loans. In this case the underwriting and other commissions to the New York syndicate headed by Messrs. J. P. Morgan & Company, amounted to 2 per cent. The Bank of Montreal was able to obtain for the Government a remission of one-quarter of one per cent upon that commission of 2 per cent, leaving the net commission to the New York syndicate one and three-quarters per cent for underwriting and other commissions and expenses.

speechtext: I think what misled my hon. friend is the fact that the $111,111 was interest upon the amount from the date it was paid until the Bank of Montreal received it in New York for our account. speechtext:
My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) made an inquiry with regard to a resolution on the Order Paper with respect to the Board of Pension Commissioners and the rates of pension. Hon. gentlemen wiR remember that on March 14, 1916, a committee was appointed for the purpose of taking into consideration the rates of pensions. On the 10th May, 1916, the committee made a unanimous report. The chairman of the committee, on the 18th May, moved that the report should be commended to the consideration of the Government. Parliament prorogued on the same day. There was not an opportunity to bring in legislation at that session.^ Accordingly, on the 3rd June, 1916, the recommendations of the committee were put into the form of an Order in Council and passed under the War Measures Act. By a resolution now on the Order Paper it was proposed that a similar committee should be appointed this year to take into consideration representations that had been made to the Government from various quarters, and more particularly by several organizations of returned soldiers, as to the desirability of increasing the rates of pensions thus allowed. This was urged for various reasons, several of which have a great deal of force. We have reached the conclusion that it would be impracticable to deal with the matter in a thorough and satisfactory manner at this session and that it is a subject which should be dealt with finally and permanently by the new Parliament which is to be summoned in the early future. There is, however, this consideration which the Government will have to take into account. Owing to the fact that since the committee made this report on May 10 last yeaT the cost of living in Canada has very appreciably increased, it is thought reasonable and desirable that, pending the consideration of this question by Parliament, there should be some increase made, that it should be made on a percentage basis and that it should take effect from the beginning of the present fiscal year, which is the first of 
April last. Accordingly, as soon as the prorogation of Parliament permits, the Government propose to take the question into consideration in that regard for the purpose of affording temporary relief at this time and with the view of having the whole question exhaustively and finally settled by a new Parliament fresh from the people as soon as that Parliament has been summoned.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER.
speechtext: Did I understand my right hon. friend to state that the Government had decided to grant an increase, and if so, what is the rate of increase?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER.
speechtext: That has not been determined. We thought the increase in the cost of living made it only fair and reasonable, as 'well as desirable, that there should be an increase, to date from the first of April last, pending consideration by a new Parliament of the whole subject in an exhaustive and final way. It seems undesirable that so important a question should be dealt with finally by this Parliament. Therefore, we propose to give temporary relief by the method which I have mentioned, .and the whole matter will then be entirely free for such disposition as the new Parliament may determine to make of it.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER.
speechtext: And the rate of that temporary increase will be determined after prorogation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER.
speechtext: We will make probably a temporary percentage increase to meet the increased cost of living in the meantime, leaving it free to the new Parliament to deal with the whole question when it comes up for their consideration and determination.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Consideration in committee of Bill No. 125, providing for the 'acquisition by His Majesty of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company-Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance-resumed from Thursday, August 23, Mr. Rainvi'lle in the Chair.-
On section 1-Acquisition of shares of Canadian Northern railway authorized:

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
When this Bill was last in committee, I made a few remarks on its merits as I understood them, but as the Government appeared to be anxious that the committee should rise and the House proceed to other business. 
I curtailed my remarks and I therefore desire to resume them. As I said then, so far as I am personally concerned, I am in perfect accord with the suggestion of taking over the Canadian Northern and its assets and properties, in the public interest. The two questions which to my mind are of paramount importance in connection with the matter are, first, the cost or price which is to be paid for the property, and, second, the system of management which is to be adopted. So far as the system of management is concerned. I have no hesitation whatever in saying that this railway system, together with the National ' Transcontinental [DOT] railway, and the Intercolonial railway, the Prince Edward Island railway, the Hudson Bay railway all the railways owned by the Government, should be put under one Board of Management which should be absolutely free and independent of all political control, and that the combined properties should te operated by such an independent 4 p.m. board on a strictly commercial basis in the interests of the public. I believe that by this means, instead of being a gigantic failure, as the Intercolonial has always proved to be, the combined systems could be operated with success and so to redound greatly to the benefit of the people and the best interests of the country.
The question of operation is not so much to be considered in connection with this Bill, because the Government apparently intend to leave the operation in the hands of the present company, under its own control and supervision. But surely that management cannot last. It can be at the best but a temporary arrangement and a new Parliament will certainly have to deal with this question. I submit that the proper way to deal with it is on the lines I have suggested.
But the question for discussion here is particularly the terms on which this property is to be acquired, and to my mind, if the public ownership of these railways is to be a success, the principal thing to' be considered is that we should first, as is said by racing men, get away to a good start; we should start right in order to be sure that we shall end right. The first consideration in starting is the cost of this property, what shall we pay for it? The Government have introduced this Bill in which they set forth that they shall acquire this property at a price to be determined by arbitration. They therefore enact in the Bill that a price shall be paid for the outstanding stock, the 600,000 shares of stock still ouistand-

ing, this price to be fixed by arbitration. My contention is that, as there is no value to that stock, there is nothing to refer to a Board of Ar-trators, and there should be no arbitration in regard to the price of these outstanding shares. The Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) the other day, when addressing himself to this question, dwelt very strongly and somewhat lengthily on the equity of redemption, contending that mere was an equ'ty of redemption in the Canadian Northern Railway Company, which had a value, which value should be fixed. He said very emphatically that if there was a foreclosure, or if the property was taken over by expropriation, there would have to be a reference to the courts to determine the value of the property and the value of equity of redemption, and whether there was a value in the equity of redemption, and he contended that the value can be fixed under this Bill by arbitration as well as in any other matter.
I submit that there is no equity of redemption, that there is no value to the stock.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: How could there be a foreclosure if there is no equity of redemption?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
There is a very simple method of foreclosure which is provided for by the statute. This method of foreclosure was pointed out in 1914 by the Government very clearly and emphatically at the time that the Act providing for the guaranteeing of the $40,000,000 of securities was under discussion. At that time I read to the House certain language of the Prime Minister in regard to the method to be adopted in acquiring this property in the event of default. After I bad concluded my remarks the Prime Minister stated that the suggestions which I had made had been frequently made on previous occasions, and as frequently answered. But I had never heard the suggestions made; much less had I heard them answered. The Minister of Finance, in his remarks on that question on Thursday last, made a similar statement. He said, however, not that these suggestions had been answered, but that they could be. He said he could very easily explain why proceedings should not be taken under section 24 of the Act of 1914 to acquire possession and control of this property. I should like to hear that explanation from the minister; I have not heard any up to this time either from him or from any other member of the Government. I have read what the Prime Minister said in 1914; let me read what the Minister of Finance said on that occasion when dealing with the subject of what method should be adopted in acquiring this property in the event of default. He said, page 3,943 of Hansard, 1914:
It I have a mortgage on a company's undertaking I do not care very much for the stock as security except that it is advisable to have the stock in order that I can take possession of the company, put in my own receiver, and operate the company with my own board of directors. That is the only advantage. The stock does not give any higher security, but it makes the realization of the security a little more convenient. What security have we? I have seen a good deal of financing in my time, and I know something of law although my hon. friend from Fictou (Mr. Macdonald) does not think so, and I want to say this: I have never seen as effectual a means of entering into possession of a property upon which a mortgage is held as has been devised by the Solicitor General in connection with this transaction.
Then he goes on to say, at page 3,944:
I was dealing with the question of remedy upon default, and was pointing out that we have a much better control than would be afforded by the security of a majority or all of the stock of the Canadian Northern. What have we? Upon default, the Order in Council at once becomes a rule of court, and is absolutely beyond question so far as its authority is concerned. We can displace the board of directors of any or all of the companies bydirectors of our own choice, who are given power to carry on the road as provided in the resolutions, and it is open to the Government through Parliament to deal with that road by way of sale or otherwise, as may be expedient and in the public interests. It can be sold in whole or in part to a corporation, or it can be operated in the interests of the public of Canada.
I call upon the Minister of Finance to explain why he does not, under that Act, take over that property and operate it in the interests of the public of Canada. There is nothing to prevent his doing so; in fact, the majority report of the Drayton-Acworth Commission recommends it. At page LXXXIV, the commissioners say:
In the case of the Canadian Northern Railway Company no proceedings in court are requisite. Under the provisions of section 24 of the Canadian Northern Railway Guarantee Act, 1914, the Governor General in Council has power, when authorized by Parliament, to declare by order, if default is made by the company in payment of interest on the $45,000,000 guaranteed securities (the interest on which is at present being found by the Government) that the equity of redemption of the company is absolutely barred and foreclosed; and thereupon the whole property becomes vested in His Majesty in right of the Dominion of Canada.
I cannot understand what explanation the minister can make of his present atti-

tude on this question, having regard to these recommendations made by the commissioners!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: If my hon. friend will turn to page LVIII of the Drayton-Acworth report he will find the recommendation that the trustees acquire this stock, just as we propose to acquire it, and continue the company as a going concern. They say that if the company is not willing to do that it can be forced to do it under the legislation of 1914. They suggest that the Canadian Northern Railway stock should be conveyed to the trustees precisely as we have determined that it shall he conveyed to the Dominion Government.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Assuming that the minister is right in that, why does he not go further? If it is his desire to carry out the suggestions of the commissioners in one particular, why not carry them out in other particulars? The commissioners say, it is true, that the trustees should acquire the stock, but they say, also, that the stock has absolutely no value; they do not recommend that the trustees pay anything for it. If the Canadian Northern refuses to hand over the stock, which the commissioners say they should do without consideration, the Government can exercise their right under section 24 of the Act of 1914. Let the Government carry out the suggestion of the commissioners. Let them say to the Canadian Northern Railway Company: You must hand over that 600,000 shares of stock; if you do not do so, we will take proceedings under section 24 of the Act of 1914. The commissioners say not only that the shares are of no value, but that the liabilities against the property are many millions more than the property is worth. They do suggest, however, that a sort of honorarium ought to be given to Mackenzie and Mann for their services, their time and trouble; they mention $1,500,000 worth of stock as being the maximum consideration in that regard. There is no suggestion that Mackenzie and Mann or the Canadian Northern Railway Company should receive cash. They say that as Mackenzie and Mann have devoted much time and trouble to the building of a good road through a prosperous section of the country, the Government might reasonable consider it fair and equitable to give them some compensation for their years of labour. But what are the Government doing? They are referring to a board of arbitration the question of what

value shall be given to these shares at the time of the signing of the agreement between the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Government.
The Government is actually suggesting that there is a value or price of some kind to be put on the shares, and no doubt the Canadian Northern will suggest that to their counsel who appear before the arbitrators. They will say to the arbitrators: There is some value in these shares; it is for you to fix what that value is. That value, moreover, is to be fixed as of the time the agree ment is signed, and at a time that agreement is signed, those shares will have a very much greater value than they have at the present time. If they have no value at the present time, the mere fact that the Government is taking over the property, assuming all the liabilities, gives a value to those shares which Messrs. Drayton and Acworth say have no value. Why should not the findings of this Royal Commission be accepted by the Government? The Royal Commission was composed of expert railwaymen. Mr. A. H. Smith, president of the New York Central Railroad, is one of the best railway men in America; Mr. W. M. Acworth is one of the leading authorities on railway matters, and Sir Henry Drayton is undoubtedly a man of experience in railway matters. They have gone into this question fully, impartially and with a desire to ascertain definitely and to put before the country clearly the true situation in regard to the whole railway problem in Canada, and to recommend to the Government and to the Canadian people what should be done in that regard in view of existing conditions. What do they find?
1 have already given the findings in this House and they might be stated again, because at the present time there is not any question of as great importance as this railway question. It is a matter that must be grappled with courageously and dealt with frankly, honestly and squarely in the interest of the people of this country. This is a gigantic undertaking for the people of Canada to assume, and it will require careful and honest management. This Royal Commission ascertained the value of the property from three different aspects. In the first place they valued it as a cash investment, the cash actually put into the property, and they found that to amount to $383,302,451. There is no reason in the world why any one should dispute the accuracy of those figures. The commission had the best men they could get to aid them in their inquiry, and I have not heard of those figures being disputed, even by the

Canadian Northern Railway Company. They also say:
We And then $370,000,000 to be the maximum possible cost of the Canadian Northern system as at present existing-. In other words, as indeed is frankly admitted- by Canadian Northern witnesses, the Canadian Northern shares represent no cash investment.
They also ascertained the value on the physical basis, and they say that the actual value of the road on a physical basis in its present condition is $357,409,678, and that -the equipment is at the present time worth $45,339,985, making a total of $402,749,663. Then they ascertained the value of the property as a going concern, and on that basis they say that the shares have absolutely no value. In view of all that, if the Government is desirous of dealing with this matter fairly, and honestly in the interest of the people who are to own the road, I cannot understand why the Government should assert that there is a value to those .shares.
On Thursday last the Minister of Finance stated that there had been something like $65,000,000 of an error made in the calculations of the Royal Commision; that there was about $25,000,000 of liabilities which had been added which should not have been added, and that there was about $40,000,000 of assets which had not been considered. I understand that is quite incorrect. I understand that those assets and liabilities, so called, were considered by the Royal Commission, and I believe, before the discussion on this Bill is concluded, it will be shown conclusively -that those assets and liabilities were taken into consideration and were dealt with along with the other assets and liabilities of the company. But, supposing there had -been an error as is suggested, what would the effect be? We find that the actual value of the property as ascertained by the Royal Commission is $370,000,000. What are the liabilities? According to the balance sheet of last year the liabilities of the Canadian Northern, leaving out the stock and a balance of about $39,000,000 which they claim as a profit, we have the actual liabilities of the company as $438,000,000. Assuming for a moment that there is an error of $65,000,000, that will leave $373,000,000 as the liabilities which the people of Canada will assume in taking over this property. The Royal Commissioners say that, under no possible circumstances, could the property have cost more than $370,000,000, so that even supposing there had been an error of
$65,000,000, as is contended, there is still a surplus of liabilities, over any -money which could have been put into the road, of more than $3,000,000.
That being so, I really cannot understand why the Government is deliberately attempting to give several million dollars more to these men or to their creditors- because that is what it will mean. I have no desire that Mackenzie and Mann should be dealt with harshly, but we must remember that Mackenzie and Mann took the chances of keeping all the stock in their own hands and of financing this great system by government guarantees and bonuses and land grants, without putting one dollar of their own private money into the enterprise, or paying one dollar for the stock. If Mackenzie and Mann had in the beginning associated with themselves some strong financial man who were really interested in railway operation, and if these men had put their money into the system and paid something for the shares, I would feel that they were entitled to get something out of it. But Mackenzie and Mann have financed the road altogether on public money. Not one dollar of their own money has gone into the road, and what is mores Mackenzie and Mann were the contractors who built the road for the company at their own price. Mackenzie and Mann gave the contract for building the road to themselves at their own price; there was no competition whatever, and they then sublet the work to other contractors, undoubtedly at a figure which would yield them a profit on the work. I, for one, do not believe that Mackenzie and Mann during all these years have not made money for themselves out of this gigantic enterprise. It is absolutely unbelievable. I cannot believe it myself, nor do I think any man in this country will believe it. Mackenzie and Mann themselves have never taken the trouble to deny it. It is true that Mr. Mitchell and Mr. Hanna have stated that the books of the company do not show that any money has been paid to Mackenzie and Mann, but every one knows that there are a thousand-and-one ways in which money can be paid out without it appearing in the books of the company as having been paid to any particular person, and until I see their statement under oath, I, for one, cannot and will not believe ihat Mackenzie and Mann have made no profit out of this enterprise from the beginning up to the present time.
I have given as distinctly as I could the views I hold on this question. As I



have said, it is a gigantic undertaking for the people of Canada to assume. We are running up in this country an enormous indebtedness in consequence of this disastrous war, but even before the war, there was an enormous increase in our public debt, and it behooves us who represent the people in this Parliament to take the greatest possible care that the indebtedness of Canada is not unduly and unnecessarily increased. By the taking over of this property we shall be adding enormously to our burdens. We are actually assuming a burden of many million dollars more than the property costs or could be duplicated for to-day, and on top of that, the Government is suggesting that Mackenzie and Mann have an equity of redemption in this property. Notwithstanding what has been said by the Royal Commissioners, the Government suggests that these shares have a value, and that the value should he fixed by arbitration. I deprecate as strongly as I can any- such suggestion. I say that the Government should act under section 24 in the manner they told this Parliament they would act. The Government in 1914 took credit for having so carefully safeguarded the interests of the people, and pledged themselves to the people of Canada that if default took place, they would take over the property and operate it, so the Minister of Finance said, " in the interests of the public of Canada." I call on the Government now to carry out in good faith the pledge which they made at that time, and which was embodied in the Aot of 1914. It is perhaps well that I should read section 24, in order that the matter may be fully understood:
If authorized by the Parliament of Canada, the Governor in 'Council may on such terms and conditions (if any) as Parliament may prescribe, at any time while any event of default shall exist and be continuing, by order declare the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern and of all other persons whomsoever in the mortgaged premises to he foreclosed, and thereupon the equity of redemption of the Canadian Northern (and of such other persons) in the mortgaged premises and every part thereof shall he and become absolutely barred and foreclosed, and the same shall thereupon he vested in His Majesty in right of the Dominion of Canada.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
knew that there was an equity of say, one million dollars, coming to Mackenzie and Mann, would he advocate that the Government rob Mackenzie and Mann of that amount and put it in the treasury?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.

If there was an equity of a million dollars coming to Mackenzie

Well, because of that and of the other reasons I have mentioned, I consider it my duty to state to the House my views on the question and my reasons for supporting the policy of the Government. I do so with a great deal of confidence and satisfaction, because I feel that the measure the Government has presented to the House and to the country is a proposal which, when properly grasped by the people of the country, will meet with general approval. I support the measure because it marks a new era in the railway history of Canada. It is a step forward towards the acquisition of the control and direction and the ownership of the great railway systems of Canada beginning by taking over the second largest system, the Canadian Northern Railway, a system comprising some ten thousand miles of road. The main burden of the criticisms of hon. gentlemen opposite against the Government has been " why does it not act under section 24 of the Bill of 1914?" They suggest that for some sinister reason the Government is seeking to evade the powers given to it by Parliament under that Bill. I would like to call the attention of the committee to the wording of the section referred to:
If authorized by Parliament the Governor in Council may on such terms and conditions, if any, as Parliament may prescribe foreclose the equity of redemption_etc.
In other words section 24 of the Act of 1914 lays upon this Parliament the responsibility of saying in what manner the terms of the agreement shall be enforced or taken advantage of. That is exactly what the Government is doing. It comes before the House now after three years of war intervening since the passing of that Act, and says to Parliament: "This is what we recommend having in view the circumstances with which we are surrounded and the conditions which have been brought about because of the war since the passing of the Act of 1914." The idea is exactly what hon. gentlemen opposite have been urging upon the Government, namely the securing of control of the road. It is quite true that the method taken is not precisely that suggested in clause 24, but it is useless for hon. gentlemen to split hairs, legally speaking, over the question of foreclosure of the equity of redemption as against the purchase of the stock. Any hon. gentleman knows, who knows the law that if you foreclose a mortgage, the mortgagor has some right to be heard in that foreclosure. That

is a principle which runs through all British law, and hon. gentlemen opposite know it very well.

I simply draw attention to a fact, which no amount of argument will dispel. The fact is there and I say there is ground for appeal against that law in that way. However, we will pass this over for a moment.
What do we get from hon. gentlemen opposite to help us out of this dilemma which they say we are in? What are the suggestions? Two or three suggest a receivership. Others suggest that we dispose of the assets of this company; others suggest liquidation, and still others suggest that we give them further loans and see if they will not work out their own salvation. All these suggestions have been made in a cursory manner not with any degree of seriousness and simply with a desire to confuse the issue which is now before Parliament.
Let me call attention to some of the suggestions which have been made. The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) said very emphatically that we required three transcontinental railways in Canada. The hon. member for Rouville says that:
The Government has no mandate to commit the country to the immediate completion of that third transcontinental railway.
The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea), following along that line, said the other day:
I am bound to say that whoever were responsible for two transcontinental railways being
,'5-Ir. Stevens.]
built, east of Port Arthur and some distance west of Edmonton, were very much lacking in judgment.
His own leader says:
I accept fullest responsibility for the policy -that this country required no less than three lines of railway.
With such a conflict of views as this, with no seriousness in the suggestions or criticisms, I ask what are we to accept as the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite in connection with this matter.
I wish to discuss one policy suggested by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) very frequently in the numerous times that he has addressed the committee. He has suggested that a valuation be made of the physical assets of the road, and that they be disposed of and divided among the security-holders.
That is suggested by the hon. member for St. John. I would like to ask him, or the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), how they propose to make this disposition of the assets of the road. Would they sell the track to one person, the rolling stock to another, the telegraph company to some one else and the express company to some one else, or would they sell the road as a going concern? If they are going to dispose of the road as a going concern, to whom would they dispose of it? There is only one company to whom they could dispose of it. I have a great deal of respect for the views of a corporation lawyer on matters appertaining to corporation rights, but I question the judgment of gentlemen who are corporation lawyers, when they are dealing with what is in the interest of the public in conflict with that which is in the interest of corporations. While I have a great deal of respect for the opinion of some of these hon. gentlemen, I question their judgment in a matter of this kind. I, ask how they are going to dispose of this road and to whom? If they are going to dispose of the institution as a going con-* cern, there is only one buyer, that is known to the country, and that is the Canadian Pacific railway. Either the Government must take over this system or the Canadian Pacific railway will take it over. The hon. member f-or St. John could not have been' serious when he suggested that the assets be disposed of and divided amongst the security holders. That, of course, is impossible.
Let ns look for a moment at the only possible manner of carrying out this suggestion, by disposing of it to the Canadian Pacific railway. Every one knows, and I

think the financial interests of this country particularly know, that the Canadian Pacific Railway is exceedingly anxious to acquire this system and that it would pay very handsomely for it. I think I am quite safe in saying that Lord Shaughnessy would not deny that there were negotiations to this end. But, Sir, the question that this House and this committee must ask is: Is it in the interest of Canada that the Canadian Pacific railway should acquire this system? I submit that there are only two alternatives. One is that the Government must take it and the other is that the Canadian Pacific railway should take it. Before an amalgamation can take place between any of the great railway systems in Canada, if I remember aright, the approval of Parliament must be secured, or at least	the	approval of	the	Gov.ernment.	The	only thing	that standsbetween	the	amalgamation of	theCanadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific railway is the Government. If the Government gave its approval, this amalgamation might, take place. I hold that the	time	has arrived	when	this
Parliament should be thoroughly seized of this fact and should make it utterly impossible, for the time being and in the future, for the Canadian Pacific railway to control the Canadian Northern system. On the other hand, I claim that this is the time to take the first great step towards the nationalization of railways in Canada.
A great deal has been said on this debate as to the gifts and assistance that have been given to the Canadian Northern. It is quite right that we should take all these things into consideration. But it is well that we should ask ourselves the question, when dealing with the Canadian Northern railway, as it is being constantly compared with the Canadian Pacific railway:	What
placed the Canadian Pacific railway in the strong position which it occupies in Canada to-day. Was it built out of the money of the investors? The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), who has just taken his seat, spent a considerable time attacking the Canadian Northern promoters because they had not put, as he said, one cent of their own money into the system. As a matter of fact, they put in some money, but not .anything like the full amount required. Did the promoters of the Canadian Pacific railway put their own money -into the system to any great extent? Let us look at some of the figures. I find that the Canadian Pacific railway have received from the Dominion and the provinces:
Cash subsidies	$ 67,000,000 -
Lands sold	 123,800,000
Lands unsold	 119,250,000
For surveys by Gov., etc.. ..	37,750,000

In all, they have received gifts to the value of $337,000,000. As a matter of fact,
I am informed that the figure is greater than that but that figure is quite sufficient for the point I intend to make. The interest on the $67,000,000 of cash subsidies granted to the Canadian Pacific railway at 4J per cent amounts to in the neighbourhood of $3,000,000 annually. If you take the interest for thirty years you will find that nearly $100,000,000 of interest has been thus placed in the coffers of the Canadian Pacific railway. I include this interest for this reason:	The guarantees given to the Canadian Northern, of which I shall say something later on, are interest bearing and they have to pay the interest out of earnings from year to year. The gifts to the Canadian Pacific railway bear no inte*est. The value of the money is in the road and they have to pay no interest upon it. Then, we have this result, that the Canadian Pacific railway cost $354,000,000 according to the statement in their last balance sheet. That is for the road exclusive of equipment.
In other words, they have received in cash bonuses from this country, as a free gift, outright, from the people of Canada, a sum almost equal to the total cost of their road. Let us look at the corresponding figures for the Canadian Northern railway. They have received total cash subsidies from all sources of $38,800,000 as against $68,000,000 cash subsidies to the Canadian Pacific railway. Then they have realized from the cash sale of lands, and realized by way of debenture bonds, $34,000,000, a total of approximately $73,000,000, which they have received in outright gifts from this country this amount. In addition to that, they have equity in land to the value of $4,000,000 still in hand, or .a total of gifts of $78,400,000, as against $337,000,000 given to the Canadian Pacific railway. This should be taken into consideration when we compare these two great systems. To proceed with this comparison in another way, let me point out that in the Canadian Pacific railway annual statement, and also in the Drayiton-Acworth report, we find that the Canadian Pacific railway still have 11,500,000 acres of land, including townsites, etc., in their possession. Much of this is in localities close to transportation, close to

towns and villages, and in arable districts suitable for cultivation. They also show in the same balance sheet cash on hand of $57,000,000, and in addition to that $23,000,000 as a reserve against contingencies. I therefore ask if it would not be desirable, in this age and time, when there is such a demand for increase of production, that instead of holding these arable lands, the gift of the people of Canada, the Canadian Pacific railway should spend, or invest, its contingency reserve of $23,000,000 in the development of some of these lands close to the towns, cities and villages of Western Canada? That is a suggestion which I think is quite in order, and one that might well be considered by the Canadian Pacific railway. I go further. In 1909 the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who was then in power, and his Government, gave to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company the right to issue an additional block of stock amounting to $30,000,000. This was issued at $125 when the stock was selling on the market at $184, netting to the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company $17,700,000. Then, in January, 1912, by the Act of 1911, another $18,000,000 was distributed at $150, when the stock was selling at $236 on the market, making another gift to the Canadian Pacific railway shareholders of $15,000,000. The reason I cite this, and the reason I draw attention to these figures which I have already cited, is that these gifts were given to the Canadian Pacific railway because it was known that, in the earher periods of construction, they would have difficulty in paying their way without levying exorbitant freight rates. The object in the construction of the railway was to encourage the transportation of goods throughout Canada. The object of the Canadian Northern railway is exactly the same, to encourage the development of the transportation facilities of this country and to keep down freight rates within reasonable bounds. But instead of applying the gifts of the country for the purpose of keeping down freight rates, these gifts have been used by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for the sole purpose of swelling the dividends of its shareholders. .
The suggestion is made that we should allow the Canadian Northern railway to go into the hands of a receiver. I must say, to give credit to most of the hon. gentlemen opposite, that this has not been
CMr. Stevens.]
received with any very great 5 p.m. favour. But this' has been suggested, and my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) said that he was thoroughly in favour of it, although he bowed to the wishes of the majority. I simply wish to point out that if this road were allowed to go into liquidation or into the hands of a receiver, it would have an exceedingly serious effect on the credit of the country. Not only that, it would dissipate or destroy, to a large degree, the value of the organization built up by the Canadian Northern railway system. It is just as impossible successfully to follow out the policy suggested by the hon. member from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), namely, to dispose of the assets of the road and divide them among the security holders, as it is to let it go into the hands of a receiver.
Our great object at this time is to do two things, first to preserve the transportation facilities that have been developed in Western Canada and, second, to do this with as little loss as is possible. I am quite satisfied with the arbitrator appointed by the Government, that is Sir William Meredith. I do not think a fairer or more just man could be secured. I deprecate very much the reflections cast upon Sir William Meredith by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) a few minutes ago. Sir William is above reproach, one of the ablest men on the bench. This is, however, a question which affects western Canada particularly and one which perhaps a western man would understand better than an eastern man, and if I had had my way a western man would have been appointed as arbitrator; but as the Government have chosen Sir William Meredith, I am content as I think that, so far as character is concerned, no better choice could have been made.
I believe that the time has come when we should take a very broad and very generous and very deep view of this question of transportation in Canada. I believe that the time has come when all the railway systems of Canada should be taken under the control and direction of the Government. When I say all, I include the Canadian Pacific railway, because, in view of these very large grants that have been given to the Canadian Pacific railway, I am led to ask the question, has the Canadian Pacific Railway Company played the game with the country to the extent of these grants that have been given to it? Is the country getting the freight rates to

which it is entitled? Let me give the House one brief illustration of the freight rate problems that we are faced with on the Pacific coast. Up to about 1907, the Canadian Pacific railway gave the people of the Pacific coast the privilege of shipping freight 400 miles eastward as against shipments by Montreal merchants 2,600 miles westward; in other words, we paid as much to ship freight to Golden, B.C., as the merchants of Montreal paid to ship to the same point. There is no ground on which that can be justified, and yet that is what we are faced with. To-day we have the splendid privilege of shipping freight as far as Calgary, 600 miles, against the Montreal merchant shipping to Calgary 2,300 or 2,400 miles. I cite this to show that the freight rate question of Canada is one of the most important, and that the time has come when we should ask ourselves the question: Are we getting a square deal from this enormous railway corporation in comparison with the assistance given to it by the people of Canada in these grants of land and of cash? To my mind a Board should be appointed to administer the railway affairs of this country and to pay to the stockholders of the different railways taken over a fair and reasonable dividend. If you examine the reports of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for as many years back as you care to go, you will find that these land subsidies that we gave to them for the purpose of minimizing the freight rates of the company have simply been spent in giving dividends to the shareholders and swelling the price of the stock of the company. I have no objection to the earnings of the Canadian Pacific railway being used up as dividends, but I do object to the proceeds of subsidies given by the people of this country being used in that manner.
We have a further suggestion from the honourable member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) which I wish to consider for a very few moments. He says that the Government should expropriate the railway and the rolling stock of the company, and nothing more; that we should leave the company in existence; leave it its stock and its liabilities. His suggestion is that we should take possession of the physical assets of the road, but that we should let the company keep its organization, its officials, its telegraph and express companies-all the things that make the operation of a railway possible. But how would possession of the railway and its rolling stock
be acquired ? In order to take over the road and the rolling stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company you would have to float a new government loan. It may be interesting for the committee to note the price paid by the Canadian Northern Railway Company for its money. For instance, the company floated loans amounting to $270,000,000 in Great Britain at a cost of 4 -347 per cent. Where could we get money at that rate or anything like that rate to-day? Honourable gentlemen on the other side have criticised the Government because they had to pay six per cent and more for a loan in the New York market. Yet they suggest that we should expropriate the physical assets of this road, purchase them outright, and leave the company in existence. I mention this merely to show how absurd it is to suggest that at this time we expropriate the road and pay off the securities to any considerable extent.
It has been suggested'by the member for St. John and others that the $147,000,000 of unsecured bonds of the Canadian Northern Railway Company should not cause the Government any anxiety, that, if there is not sufficient	money to pay for
them, they should be allowed to go. It	is suggested that, as these bonds
were sold at a very low rate, no serious loss would be involved if this course was adopted. As a matter of fact, $110,000,000 of the $147,000,000 of unsecured bonds were sold at about 96 on the British market, or at a cost to the company of 4j per cent- which is a very favourable issue. Moreover, practically the full amount of the issue of these bonds went into the road. Of the land grant bonds, $12,250,000 were sold in Great Britain at 94, the net cost to the company being 4-98 per cent. The proceeds of these, as well as of those that were sold in this country, went into the road. Notwithstanding these facts, hon. gentlemen opposite suggest that the Government should repudiate those bonds. This is what the member for St. John says:
There are something like $147,000,000 of securities which are not guaranteed by the Dominion or the provinces. I presume these [DOT] securities are held by strong financial men, by bankers and others, who could afford to lose a portion of their securities.
1 submit that it is unworthy of a member of this committee to suggest that simply because these bonds may be held by individuals who can afford to lose them, the country should repudiate its responsibilities and allow the bonds to go by

default. My contention is that the full proceeds of the bond and land sales of the Canadian Northern Railway Company have gone into the road. So far as we can gather from a most careful scrutiny of the accounts of the company-I myself have gone over them carefully, and I know that other gentlemen have done so-the proceeds of the sale of securities of this road have gone into its construction, none being diverted to other uses. That being the case, it is fair and reasonable that this country should recognize and accept the full responsibility of those securities. If, as suggested by the member for St. John, the bonds had been sold at 50, there would be some reason for asking for an' adjustment. But in view of the fact that they were sold at 96 and 98, there is no reason why we should repudiate any portion of the unsecured bonds of the company.
In 1914 the leader of the Opposition and the member for St. John suggested that in the legislation then being enacted we should insert a provision that the maximum purchase price of the stock should be $30,000,000. I assume that that suggestion was made eeriouely. It was not thought desirable, however, to accept the suggestion, at that time, because practically all the members of the House, especially the western members, expected that the Canadian Northern Railway Company would be able to pull itself out of its financial difficulties. Within a month or so after the House prorogued war broke out, and from that day to this it has been utterly impossible for the Canadian Northern or any other corporation to do its financing in Great Britain or in New York. But although this suggestion was not accepted in 1914, there is no reason why the principle should not be adopted to-day, in view of the changed circumstances. There is, however, this difference: At that time it was suggested that the value of the stock might well be set at $30,000,000. Here we make no limitation. Hon. gentlemen may say: Why do you not fix a maximum price? But if the Government had put in a maximum price of $5,000,000,	$10,000,000, or any other
amount, hon. gentlemen opposite-the member for St. John, the member for Pictou and others.-would have alleged that the Government intended to give Mackenzie and Mann that amount of money. The only sane and proper method is to leave the arbitrators absolutely free and untramelled in coming to a decision in this matter. I suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite who
[Mr. Stevens. 1
object to this Bill that the measure is a fair one; that it will give the country a railway system second only to the Canadian Pacific Railway system, and that it will be the first step in Canada towards the nationalization of railways.	_
Not only will it do that, but it will introduce that system in a manner that will enable us to work it out free from party patronage, so far as that is possible. I join with many others who have said previously in this debate that, if it is humanly possible, political and party patronage should be eliminated from the administration of the railways of Canada, and I believe there is a genuine effort to do that, I believe further the people of this country desire it.
We are faced with one issue-shall the Canadian Pacific railway control this country by owning the railway systems of the country, or shall the Government enter upon a project of a Government-owned railway system? That is the clear issue before us, and there is no use in disguising the fact. I am going to read to the committee extracts from an editorial on the front page of the Toronto Star, and I do not think any hon. genlteman will charge the Toronto Star with being a Tory paper, or prejudiced in favour of the Government, or, in any sense, tramelled in its opinions, because if it is one thing, it is radically democratic. I will read a few extracts from this editorial in order to impress upon the committee, much more forcibly than my own arguments would do, the seriousness of the present situation and the necessity of Parliament facing it, in order that the committee may realize that the time has come when we must choose between the continuation of corporate control and direction or government ownership and direction of railways. The editorial says:
The decision of the Government to take over the Canadian Northern railway and also its express and telegraph systems is, we believe, an absolutely right one, and if the details of the plans put forward need to be improved, Parliament is in session for the very purpose of doing such work in the public behalf.
That, I think, is worthy of consideration. I am willing to join with any hon. gentleman in improving the details of this Bill, but what we should do is to suggest any improvements that we think should be made, and not generally, as has been largely done in the criticism offered, to damn the Bill. The editorial goes on:
It is necessary that in Parliament, the press and throughout the country, every force favourable to public ownership should now be

exerted, because against the Government in this matter is being exerted all the influence possessed by the Canadian Pacific railway and all its allied interests. It is a formidable power that confronts the Government to prevent the nationalization of the Canadian Northern railway and its subsidiary companies. It is a power that does not hesitate to believe that it can pull down governments when it undertakes to do so.
Then it says further on:
The country has long enough been owned by the railways. It is time the railwaps were owned by the country-for the country has pretty well paid for them.
In view of the huge figures that I have given, namely, $337,000,000 as a gift to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the other figures we have heard so often, that clause has particular significance. The editorial goes on:
Every Liberal member of Ottawa who professes to believe in public ownership ought to show it now, and, instead of obstructing Canadian Northern railway purchase because of certain details, should strive to remedy defects and aid the Government in putting through this railway nationalization project.. . . Aside from party altogether there is before the country a straight public ownership issue. The Government proposes to take over the Canadian Northern railway. Opposition to this action is led by the Canadian Pacific railway and allied interests, and the aim is to prevent public ownership of the railway, express, and telegraph services concerned. People need make no mistake. If the Canadian Northern rail-wap were allowed to go into liquidation, if it dropped into a receivership, it would bounce from there into the hands of the Canadian Pacific railway.
That is exactly what I have been trying to point out this afternoon, namely, that if we allow this road to go into the hands of the receivers, into liquidation, or if we dispose of it in any other way, there is Only one place where it can drop and that, as the Toronto Star says, is into the lap of the Canadian Pacific railway. That is where the influences opposing this Bill so potently and forcibly throughout this country are so anxious to have it drop. They know perfectly well, if the present Bill can be defeated, if it can be delayed or put off, the chances of working up a measure which will bring about such a condition will, so far as the Canadian Pacific railway is concerned, be exceedingly bright.
It is suggested, in connection with the proposed amalgamation with the Canadian Pacific-and I commend this to my hon. friends from Western Canada in particular -that inasmuch as the Canadian Northern and Grand Trunk Pacific railways cannot handle the freight to-day at the present
rates and show a profit, there should be allowed an increase of 10 per cent in freight rates. That is not an unreasonable suggestion, but let us look at it for a moment.
If you allow a 10 per cent increase in freight rates to the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific, you will have at the same time to give it to the Canadian Pacific. Such an increase would mean an additional $30,000,000 from the shipping public of Canada. How much of that would go info the coffers of the Canadian Pacific? Exactly $18,000,000. The Canadian Pacific are paying a dividend of 10 per cent; they have $119,000,000 worth of lands unsold yet, and they have, therefore, no need of that increase at all. I suggest that the Government take over the Canadian Northern Railway Company and carry it on at the present freight rates. If there is a loss of, say, $12,000,000 on the operation of the Canadian Northern railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific let us foot the bill. Instead of the people of Canada paying $18,000,000 into the coffers of the Canadian Pacific, let us by a direct payment from the public treasury make up any deficit in the freight rates of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and Grand Trunk Pacific. That is an infinitely better proposition than increasing the freight rates,, because, as the saying is, the people pay the piper, and the $30,000,000 will come out of the pockets of tne people, whether you take it directly or indirectly. Therefore, we should take the first step in government ownership and nationalization of our railways by acquiring the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. I have absolute and untramelled confidence in Sir William Meredith as a just, fair and honourable arbitrator on behalf of the people of Canada. How any hon. gentleman can, for one moment, question the fairness of an arbitration carried on under him is beyond me. If there is anything to pay it will, in all fairness, be paid, and we, as members of Parliament, and as representatives of the people of Canada are willing to see that that is done. If there is no value in those snares we may rest assured that Sir William Meredith will be the last men in Canada to declare a value where there is none.
