subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
After listening attentively to the address of my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) I think I am within the judgment of the members of -this committee when I say that his observations have made it clear to the House and to the country that the Government has decided to adopt as its defence to the criticism offered from this side of the House on the measure before the committee, abuse of the Canadian Pacific railway, or perhaps it would be more correct for me to say, attacks upon the Canadian Pacific railway. If that be the only defence that the Government has to the criticism offered,

then nobody on this side of the House, least of all the individual who is now addressing the committee, should object to the adoption of such cuttlefish methods by the Government. It is true that a campaign of this kind may for the moment becloud the issue, but it is still more true that such a campaign will not mislead the public for any length of time.
My hon. friend from Vancouver began his address by saying that there was a subtle influence at work behind the opposition to this Bill; an influence, I think he said, that was based on self-interest. I presume it is unnecessary to disavow any personal interest in my own case, but possibly it is just as well that I should do so, because I desire to make some further reference to this phase of my hon. friend's argument. What he said reminded me that after the speech delivered by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett)-a prominent supporter of the Government, and a very important member of the Conservative party-the' Government press throughout the country took sudden alarm. The day following the delivery of that address, there were numerous editorials in the Government press throughout the Dominion sounding a note of warning and urging the Government in the frankest possible terms to pay heed to what had been said by the hon. member for Calgary, and to take every possible means to safeguard the public interest in connection with this legislation. The Ottawa Journal joined in giving that warning to the Government. Within a few days, however, a change was noticed in the editorial opinions of the Government press, and then for the first time it began to be stated publicly that the opposition to this Bill came from the Canadian Pacific railway and from the Bank of Montreal. The Ottawa Journal, I think, in 'referring to the memorial presented against this measure by some of the prominent citizens of Montreal, men ranking high in the professional and business life of that city, referred to the click of the cash register. My hon. friend from Vancouver this afternoon followed very closely in. the wake of that line of argument. I am told that my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) made a refutation of that accusation at the opening of this afternoon's session.
So far as I am concerned, I certainly voice no Canadian Pacific railway interests.
I have no more interest in the Canadian Pacific railway that I have in the Canadian Northern, and in opposing this measure I am acting solely upon what I conceive to

be my duty as one of the representatives of the people. The Ottawa Citizen on Saturday last dealt very briefly with this argument advanced by the Government press, and in the course of a brief editorial had this to say:
The attempt of the Government press to create the impression that the taking over of the Canadian Northern railway system by the Government has resolved itself into a struggle between the interests represented by the C.P.R. allied with the Bank of Montreal, and the Administration, is obviously political camouflage of the most amateurish sort.
The C.P.R. may desire the defeat of the present proposal; so may the* Bank of Montreal ; so may large moneyed interests in the metropolis and elsewhere. With that the people of the Dominion need not be concerned at this time. What is of the utmost importance is that the terms of the proposed acquisition be not lost sight of in this cloud of political dust. The outstanding fact is that the Administration proposes to arbitrate a matter of sixty million dollars, more or less, and that according to the terms of the bond between the Dominion and the Canadian Northern Company in 1914 the latter, as represented now in its holders of capital stock, is not entitled to one dollar of the money of the Canadian taxpayers.
I will have occasion to refer to the question of value later on, and I need not labour that point now. I desire, however, before proceeding to refer to one or two other matters that were touched upon by the hon. member for Vancouver. May I point out that in recalling the position taken on this side of the House in 1914, my hon. friend did not fully state all the terms of the amendment that was then introduced by my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley). I will have occasion to go into that later on in my remarks, and I need not dwell upon it now. I mention it merely to point out that while my hon. friend's argument in that respect was incomplete, it was altogether in accordance with the line of argument which now emanates from the government press and from the supporters of the Government.
The hon. member for Vancouver also took occasion to give quite unnecessary testimonials of character to Sir William Meredith, who has been proposed as the Government arbitrator in this matter. I am not aware that any person on this side of the House has cast any reflection whatever on Sir William Meredith, but there is an observation that might have been made, and not having been made, I propose to make it. There is just the possibility that his political friends may overwork Sir William Meredith. It may have escaped the observation of hon. gentlemen on this
side of the House that even since the Minister of Finance announced that Sir William Meredith was to be the arbitrator in connection with the valuation of the Canadian Northern railway stock, the Ontario Government has placed Sir William Meredith at the head of another board of arbitration, and, as I say, it is just possible that his political friends, may overwork Sir William Meredith in showing their regard for him. It also is a matter of interest, I think, to make inquiry whether Sir William Meredith will be able to discharge the duties which ure sought to be cast upon him under this arbitration, since he has accepted, so the newspapers say, the appointment offered to him by the Provincial Government in connection with another matter. So much for the observations of my hon. friend from Vancouver.
In the earlier stages of this discussion hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, and I think possibly one or two hon. gentlemen opposite as well, sought to get from the Minister of Finance certain information that had not been brought down. From time to time the minister has laid upon the Table statements and correspondence containing a great deal of data of which the committee had not been previously seized, but I want to take this opportunity to point out that while a considerable amount of information has been furnished, that which has been brought down is not exact, and is by no means complete. In this connection let me remind the committee that when speaking on the 16th of the present month upon some details of this Bill, I pointed out a liability of the Canadian Northern Bailway Company with regard to the province of British Columbia, and for the information of the committee as well as that of the Minister of Finance I read an item from the Vancouver Sun of August 11 of the present year, and made inquiry regarding the liability there disclosed. We have not yet received information on that point, which is a question of such importance that I purpose to refer to it again briefly. According to the correspondence exchanged between the Prime Minister and the Premier of British Columbia there may exist an exceedingly large liability which this country is assuming in taking over the Canadian Northern Kailway Company; what I said will be found on page 4774 of Hansard, and I extract merely the portion containing the item that appeared in the Vancouver Sun of August 11, which is:

Victoria, Aug. 10.-The following telegram sent by Hon. John Oliver, minister of railways, to Sir R. L. Borden to-day:
"British Columbia has guaranteed the principal and interest on forty-seven million nine hundred and seventy-five thousand dollars of Canadian Northern Pacific railway company bonds and has contracts obligating the railway company to expend twenty-two to twenty-five millions to complete. Are the province's interests being protected? Please reply quickly.
The under-mentioned reply from Sir R. L. Borden has been received:
"The Government proposes to acquire all the capital stock of the Canadian Northern railway company which owns all the stock of the Canadian Northern Pacific railway company. Copy of the Bill now before Parliament ia forwarded to-day for your consideration. The company's obligations will remain as they were before such acquirement."
The newspaper item proceeds:
By Sir Robert Borden's telegram it will be seen that the Dominion Government assumes all the Canadian Northern railway's obligations in respect to the Canadian Northern Pacific railway, both financial and as to the completion by the latter railway of its existing contracts.
When I first drew this item to the attention of ithe committee I inquired as to the amount of the liability the Dominion of Canada was assuming in connection with' the obligation set out in this correspondence. Up to the present time, so far as I am aware, we have not received an exact statement as to that from the Government. I invite the minister to give us an exact statement in that regard while the Bill is before the committee and before we are asked to proceed to another clause. It will be within the recollection of hon. gentlemen that there was considerable discussion with reference to unpaid claims of contractors. Information was also asked on this subject. I must say information was brought down, but, like most of the information received from this railway company, it is in such general terms that it is impossible to tell what claims it covers.
I am led to refer to it again, and to repeat my request for specific information by reason of the fact that since publicity was given to the discussion of those matters in the House, contractors with unpaid claims have turned up within the precincts of the House and have told me, among others, about unpaid claims against the Canadian Northern which they had been pressing for settlement for a long time without success.
I submit it is due to this committee that the Minister of Finance should insist upon the Canadian Northern Bailway Company furnishing him with the names of the contractors who have unpaid claims, and that he should not be satisfied with a simple 
bulk statement as to the amount alleged to be still due and unpaid.
Information was also sought with regard to the outstanding liability of the company in connection with compensation for land taken for right of way, terminals, etc., and for damages in connection with the taking of such land. Again the discussion in this House has brought to the attention of people who have unpaid claims the statement made by the company regarding alleged settlements. Since the committee -last met I have been told of claims in the vicinity of Ottawa which have been standing for six or seven ye-ars, claims which the people who hold them say they -are sick and tired of pressing upon the company, and that the company continues to resort to every evasion and subterfuge in order to avoid settling. I have been told of one claim m particular in regard to which there has been an intimation made that now the Government is taking over tne Canadian Northern railway of course the company will not have to deal with the claim, but the parties interested will be obliged to look to the Government for payment. This, I may say, is in the vicinity of Ottawa. I am convinced there are others of very much larger amount in and about the city of Montreal. On a previous occasion I referred to the unsettled claims for compensation and damages for land taken in connection with the Montreal Tunnel and Terminal Company. Acting upon the representations I made to the committee on that occasion the Minister of Finance was good enough to make inquiry, and on the 23rd of the present month he submitted to the House a letter written him by one of the solicitors for the Canadian Northern Company bearing upon this subject The writer of the letter is Mr. Gerard Buel, a capable and honourable gentleman, whose acquaintance I enjoyed while he acted as Law Clerk in the Department of Railways and Canals. I have no doubt that Mr. Buel has correctly set out in his letter the information given him, but I am just as positive that the information is absolutely incorrect. Mr. Ruel's letter will be found at page 5124 of Hansard and is:
Regarding: land damages arising out of the construction of the tunnel, the situation is that at the present time outstanding claims for damages to the amount of about $50,000 are in the course of adjustment. All the land which the company has to obtain for the present terminal and the right of way has been acquired and paid for in full. Easements through the mountain have not in many cases yet been adjusted, the company claiming that owing to the dis-

tance from the surface practically no damage will be sustained. These claims are standing over by agreement until one year after the operation of the tunnel.
(Sgd.) Gerard Ruel.
Let us examine the statements made by the company in this letter. In the first place it is said that the situation at the present time is that:
Outstanding claims for damages to the amount of $50,000 are in the course of adjustment.
My observations have reference to the land taken for the purpose of this Tunnel and Terminal Railway Company both behind the mountain, and on the city side of the mountain as well as in connection with the boring of the tunnel. If this letter refers to the land embraced in that stretch of the right-of-way, then, Sir, I have no hesitation in saying, based upon my own personal knowledge, that the statement that all the outstanding claims for damages amount to about $50,000 is an absolute joke.
I know of one claim approximating $350,000 that has been made, and in connection with that claim they have offered in settlement, through the Montreal solicitors for the Canadian Northern, an amount in the vicinity of $53,000.

speechtext: I know that in settlement- of a claim made by the Hon. Mr. Rainville, ex-speaker of the Legislative Assembly of Quebec, they have paid more than $50,000.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I am speaking only of
those claims of which I have personal knowledge and in that instance alone the company's solicitors proposed a settlement on the basis of $53,000. But since the Minister of Finance gave notice of this legislation that proposal was entirely abandoned and of course they are taking the same position in Montreal that they are taking here-they will pay nothing and the country will have to pay the whole shot no matter what it is. There are two other unsettled claims in connection with the right of way of which I have personal knowledge and the aggregate of these three claims is six or seven times the amount mentioned in that letter. I have not the slightest doubt there are scores of such claims if we could only get at them. The second statement in that letter is that:
All the land which the company has to obtain for the present terminal and the right of way has been acquired and paid for in full.
That statement, in view of what I have just told the committee, is obviously untrue. It has acquired the land it is true, by taking the preliminary steps for expropriation under the Railway Act, but not only has it not paid for a large part of this land in full but for a large part of this land it has not paid anything at all, but is defying the owners by legal proceedings and by appeals after the matter has been submitted to arbitration and awards have been made against the company.
Further this letter states:
Easements through the mountain have not in many cases yet been adjusted, the company claiming that owing to the distance from the surface practically no damage will be sustained. These claims are standing over by agreement until one year after the operation of the tunnel.
Claims with respect to the easements might very easily reach up into the hundreds of thousands of dollars. I submit that even though it is correctly stated that by agreement these claims are standing over until one year after the operation of the tunnel the members of this committee have a right to know what these claims are, what they amount to, and by whom they are made in order that we may form some approximate idea and in any event that the country should know what yet remains to be settled for in connection with this class of claim. So much for that letter.
I submit generally in connection with the question of land damages and compensation, that there ought to be filed with this committee a statement in detail giving the names and the amounts of all unsettled claims, and further that until that is done we cannot properly proceed with an intelligent discussion of this Bill for the reason that neither the country nor the committee is in a position to know what the country is assuming by the adoption of this present proposal. A few days ago my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) referred to what he understood t-o be some long term contracts that had been entered into between the Canadian Northern Railway Company and certain of its permanent officers and officials. He pointed out that these contracts also established a liability that would be taken over by the country under this legislation and he asked for information on that point. If my memory serves me correctly the Minister of Finance promised to make inquiry regarding that. I too would urge upon the minister that if such inquiry has not been made, it should be made at once and that the committee should be furnished with full particulars of any contracts be they long term or short term, entered into between the

Canadian Northern and Mr. Z. A. Lash; between the company and Mr. Phippen; between, the company and Mr. McLeod; between the company and Mr. Mitchell, and, generally, between the company and all of its chief officials and officers. If that is not done, if this committee proceeds in ignorance of the state of facts in that regard, Parliament and the country may wake up, after this legislation goes through, to find that instead of getting rid of a set of men, whom the country has been led to believe will be got rid of by this legislation, these men have been fastened upon the country for a much longer term of years possibly, than if they had continued in the ordinary course to be in the service of the Canadian Northern. These long term service contracts may involve a very large sum of money but in any event, whether that be the fact or not, the point has been raised, the question has been asked, the Minister of Finance undertook to get the information. I now add my request to that of the hon. member for Welland and I urge that the information be brought down to this committee before we are asked to proceed with another clause of this Bill.
Under this same general head of information I wish to refer the minister to the observations of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) with reference to the income bond securities. As reported at page 4754 of Hansard, the hon. member for Calgary said
I am going to direct the attention of the Minister of Finance to the Income Bond Securities, that increased stock of $25,000,000 that is provided. When this country acquires this enterprise and becomes owner of its shares, the $25,000,000 stock will acquire some value, and under the legislation of 1914 it was provided that these shares might he exchanged for income bond securities up to the 1st day of January, 1919. I put this to the House in all seriousness:	If we exercise the power
under the statute of 1914, we destroy those shares and that right; but if, on the other hand, we buy these shares, we leave that right, and some people with $25,000,000 of income bond certificates, are going to be able to exchange them for Canadian Northern stock for $25,000,000.
The Solicitor General dealt with that point in the address to the hon. member for Calgary, and he challenged the statement that exchange of these securities for stock was likely to be made; in fact I think he said it was so unlikely as to be altogether improbable. I did not understand the hon. -member for Calgary to accept that view, and in view of some information that I have found in the Annual Financial Review

for 1916, I think it is very desirable that the whole matter should be cleared up. For the information of the Minister of Finance and of the committee, let me read this statement from page 516 of the Annual Review of 1916:
The Canadian Northern Railway Company.
5 per cent. 20-Tear Income Charge Convertible Debenture Stock-Secured by a general charge on properties of the Company subject to prior charges. The total amount of this stock at any time outstanding is not to exceed an amount equal to $10,000 per mile of the company's lines of railway. During the years 1916, 1917 and 1918 holders of the stock have the right to exchange their holdings for an equal amount of fully paid ordinary shares in the capital stock of the company. The interest on the stock at a rate not exceeding 5 per cent, per annum is payable on 2nd May and November, only out of the net earnings of the company. In and after 1920 the company is entitled to redeem the stock at par.
If this is the same class of security as was referred to by the -hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett), then the possibility of exchange for common stock is much more immediate than appeared to be the case when the matter was under discussion between the hon. member for Calgary and the Solicitor General, and in view of this authoritative statement by the company itself, -for I assume that the company furnished this information-that such securities may be exchanged- -for common stock in the years 1916, 1917, and 1918, I invite the Minister of Finance (to make special inquiry with regard to that and to give this committee, at the earliest possible moment, the result.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I had just finished enumerating several matters in respect of which, in my judgment, the committee and the country are entitled to further and fuller information. In respect of each of these matters I again urge the Minister of Finance to procure the information asked for and to bring it down as soon as possible. Upon that head I do not feel that at the present time any further observations -are either practical or necessary.
We often hear it said that one of the greatest evils of democratic government, particularly of a modern democracy, is the growth and power of what is popularly referred to as the moneyed interests. In my

judgment this House and this country are face to face with an evil of that kind in the legislation now before the committee. In fact, the Bill now in your hands, Sir, is such a dangerous specimen of the evil to which I have alluded, that, with your permission, I desire to trace the genesis of this Canadian Northern railway proposal and in doing so to place certain important facts, as briefly as possible before the committee.
Speaking in this debate on the 16th of the present month, I stated that the present proposal grew out of an alliance that was formed in 1911 between eighteen gentlemen who came together in Toronto and who, in the assertion of what was their political and personal right, signed a letteT defining the position which they thought the country should take in defence of the financial interests which they personally and collectively represented. That alliance and that letter form the basis of this present proposal, as I propose showing. Let me recall the names of the gentlemen who signed the letter in question; they will be found at page 4774 of Hansard of this year. They are:
Sir Edmund Walker, John L. Blaikie, W. D. Matthews, W. K. George, Z. A. Lash, W. T. White, George T. Somers, R. S. Gourlay, Sir W. Mortimer Clark, R. J. Christie, Hugh Blain, H. S. Strathy, L. Goldman, G. A. Somerville, Wellington Francis, J. D. Allan, E. R. Wood, John C. Eaton.
That group of gentlemen represented particularly the Canadian Northern Railway Company, the Canadian Bank of Commerce, and the National Trust Company, of which at that time my respected and honoured friend the Minister of Finance was the general manager. After the election of 1911 these eighteen gentlemen used their influence and were successful in having one of their number appointed Minister of Finance; I refer to the hon. gentleman who now occupies that position. Since 1911 it has been a matter of common knowledge that the three institutions to which I have referred have more than once received favours at the hands of this Government. For the purpose of understanding the present position of affairs with reference to these three business and financial institutions and their connection with the proposal now before the House, it is necessary to run over briefly the interlocking directorates of these companies. Of the original eighteen gentlemen who signed the letter to which I refer and whose names I have just read, Mr. Z. A. Lash, Mr. E. R. Wood
and Mr. W. K. George are directors of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. These three gentlemen, with Mr. W. J. Christie, are also shareholders in the Canadian Northern Railway Company.

speechtext: I think my hon. friend is mistaken as to Mr. Christie. The Mr. Christie who signed the letter was Mr. R. J. Christie, of Toronto. Mr. W. J. Christie is of Winnipeg. Their only interest is as qualifying shareholders; they have no interest in the road itself.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I am not defining their interest at the moment; they are directors of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. The Mr. Christie who is also a director is not Mr. Christie of Toronto, but Mr, Christie of Winnipeg. With that correction the statement stands. Then, of the original eighteen, Sir Edmund Walker, Mr. Z. A. Lash and Mr. E. R. Wood are directors of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, of which Sir Edmund Walker is president and Mr. Lash vice-president.
The Canadian Bank of Commerce, as hon. members are aware, are pledgees of all Mackenzie and Mann's stock for advances which have been made against it. Mr. Z. A. Lash and Mr. E. R. Wood are both directors and vice-presidents of the National Trust Company. The National Trust Company, of which the Minister of Finance was formerly general manager, has acted as a trustee between the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Government with reference to several financial transactions which have taken place during the last six years. So much for the way in which the members of that group of eighteen link up the Canadian Northern, the Canadian Bank of Commerce, and the National Trust Company with the present Government.
That does not by any means exhaust the interlocking combinations that have to be kept in mind in order properly to appreciate the legislation before the committee. In addition to those I have mentioned, there is our old friend Sir Joseph Flavelle, chairman of the Imperial Munitions Board, who is a director and the president of the National Trust Company, and who is also a director of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. Besides that gentleman we have Sir John Aird, general manager of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, a director of the National Trust Company and a joint shareholder in trust of $1,000,000 worth of stock of the Canadian Northern Railway

Company. In Parliament we have Sir Edward Kemp, who is a director of the National Trust Company, and Senators Nieholls and Richardson, who are shareholders of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, according to a statement submitted by the Minister of Finance the other day. Those three latter gentlemen will soon be called upon to pass their opinion upon this legislation. These interlocking directorates and combinations of financial interests are inimical to the public welfare. On this point, let me read this opinion of the Toronto Saturday Night, which, in its issue of August 18 last, referred at some length to the Government proposal for taking over the Canadian Northern railway:
There is a distinct feeling of uneasiness in Canada over the Canadian Northern nationalization scheme, now before Parliament. Not that the great majority of people are unfavourable to nationalization. Far from it. But there is strong objection to the terms under which this nationalization is to be effected. The question arises as to whether or not the stock of the Canadian Northern railway has a cash value, and whether or not the owners, or more properly speaking, the present holders of this sixty-thousand shares-it being generally understood that the stock long ago passed out of the hands of the promoters into the strong boxes of financial institutions which are holding it as collateral -have sufficient influence to guide the Government into paying more for the stock than it is worth.
Then, after referring, by way of comparison, to same kindred legislation in the United States, the article concludes:
Canadians are in no mood to pull the chestnuts of large financial institutions out of the fire just because they have become tied up with the Canadian Northern railway enterprise. The Federal Government may well be warned that the Canadian people are in no mood to be trifled with in this matter. The Royal Railway Commission in its report stated that the common stock of the Canadian Northern railway was of no value. Now we propose to leave it to another commission to ascertain the value of this stock. There is no disposition to treat the Mackenzie & Mann interests meanly, but as the Hon. George P. Graham suggested the other day in the House, if they are to be paid, let it take the form of a " recognition " of their services in the development of the country and not as a payment for stock which has been pronounced by experts to be of no value.
In harmony with the view expressed by the Toronto Saturday Night, my hon. frieud from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) a few days ago read in the House a memorial from a group of leading financiers and professional men of Montreal, all of them I believe, without exception, strong supporters of the present Administration. In connection with that memorial, the hon. member also read an editorial from the

Montreal Gazette, one of the most outspoken supporters, in the press of this country, of the present Administration. Both memorial and editorial endorsed the position taken by the Toronto Saturday Night. To these opinions of important newspapers and citizens of Canada, may I be permitted to add that of the Montreal Star, a newspaper which, although claiming to be independent in its politics, yet manages to give an unvarying, I might say almost unbroken support to the Conservative party and which has given that support to the present Administration. The Montreal Star, in its issue of August 21, 1917, says:
Next to the war measures, by far the most important legislation before the Canadian Parliament is the Railway Bill. A wise solution of the railway problem means untold millions to Canada at a critical time in her history.
Owing to the financial embarrassments of the roads the Government was forced either to put into a receiver's hands both the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific, or to advance them more millions. It has made its choice. The Government is to give the Grand Trunk Pacific another lift of $7,500,000, and proposes to acquire the Canadian Northern stock at an arbitrated value. Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann during twenty-five years of railway exploitation, have proven their great ability as lobbyists. They have usually been able to persuade both the Liberals and Conservatives that Bills on their behalf presented to Parliament should become law without anything more than sham criticism. None of the politicians have seriously found fault with them so long as they could procure the adhesion of a majority of both parties in Parliament, and so they have had plain sailing. Every one saw that the crisis was only a question of time.
The Bill now before Parliament intended for the relief of Mackenzie and Mann and their creditors is decidedly weak in some of its provisions and dangerous in the extreme. Under the Bill as introduced there might be a staggering award. Mackenzie and Mann know how to engineer their schemes ; they must not be permitted to engineer the country into bankruptcy. It is too big a risk and there is danger that Parliament may be woefully negligent in this case, as it always has been with railway legislation.
So far there is no provision for securing honest surrender of the assets. Some have been left out of the official lists. For one of the largest subsidiary assets of the concern no adequate provision is made, and there are many other assets paid for by Government money that are not included.
If this relief Bill for the extrication of Mackenzie and Mann is to be raised above suspicion there must be provision for all the deliberations of the arbitrators to be open to the public and for the presence before the board of independent counsel representing ordinary taxpayers of Canada as distinguished from those who sit in Parliament to protect the railway interests, and there should also be a sweeping clause in the Bill that will guarantee the country against deception, and a sworn detailed schedule of assets, with a clause entitling the country to all assets omitted.

Once Mackenzie and Mann are settled with and they surrender to the Government the key to the company's secrets there may be a surprise for the country compared with which past disclosures have been mere trivialities and the country may come to realize that it has bought a white elephant that will cost millions every year.
Having regard to the fact that that article is published on the front page of a newspaper enjoying the standing of the Montreal Star, I must assume that the last paragraph in particular has been written with full knowledge of some secrets not disclosed, but which, the article says, when disclosed, will be of a character compared with which past disclosures have been mere trivialities, and the country may realize that it has bought a white elephant that will cost many millions every year.
As one of the representatives of the people I have read that article several times, and I have thought over it long and seriously. Personally, I do not know what is referred to in that last paragraph, but I want to say this, in all candour, in all honesty, and in all friendliness to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance: If he knows what that paragraph refers to, then as an honourable and an honest man-and he is both -I would a6k him to disclose that knowledge to this committee and to the House. If he does not know, then I would ask him to call upon the newspaper in which that article appeared to inform him, and through him to inform the country, what is meant by that statement. I would ask him particularly to ascertain whether the writer of that article is hinting at the possibility of the Bank Act having been contravened, and of advances having been made by the Canadian Bank of Commerce which that bank is not authorized to make under the Bank Act; and if so, whether the writer means that this legislation is the method adopted to get that bank out of the difficulty in which such a contravention of the Bank Act would involve it. It has been suggested to me that that is a con&tTuetion which could be placed upon that paragraph. I do not place such a construction upon it because I do not know enough about it, but I say to my honourable friend that having regard to the standing of the newspaper which published that article, and to the seriousness of the statements which it contains, it is in my judgment incumbent upon him to exhaust every means to ascertain what the writer of that article refers to, and to acquaint this committee, and this House, and through both, this country 315
with the information which seems to be in the possession of the writer of that article in the Montreal Star. If that is not done, then matters that now are wholly within the realm of suspicion will pass out of that realm and statements will be made which in the interests of our country should not be made. The danger, such as it is at the present time, confronting us through these interlocking directorates and the grouping of these financial interests will be small compared with the danger with which we shall be faced if the statements made in that article are not probed to the bottom, and if the fullest possible information is not procured, and communicated to the House and to the country.
Passing from that, let me direct the attention of the committee for a very brief space to the statute of 1914. That statute has been referred to by several speakers who have precided me in this debate. It was referred to by my honourable friend from Vancouver this afternoon. It has been recalled to this committee and to the House that when this statute was passed (the statement was made that within its,four corners there was provided a method for ending the dealings of Parliament and the country with the Canadian Northern, that if default should occur no further legislation and no further action would be necessary, because everything that would need to be done was provided for within the four corners of that statute. Now, when default has occurred, the Government chooses to ignore that statute. It is true that the Solicitor General proceeded in a general w&y to argue that, having regard to the present legislation the Government was, practically speaking, proceeding under the statute of 1914, and my hon. friend from Vancouver argued somewhat in the same way this afternoon. But may I recall to the committee that When the Minister of Finance introduced this legislation on the first of the present month, he never made mention of the statute of 1914, nor did he in a single word or syllable that he uttered pretend that the present legislation before this committee was in any way based upon that statute. In the course of his address on the day in question, answering an inquiry of my hon. friend from Rouville, he directed him for the information sought to the schedule of that statute, and that was the only reference made to the statute of 1914 by the Minister of Finance when he was introducing this legislation. So I say that the Minister of Finance, represent-



ing the Government-because he is responsible for this legislation, and not the Solicitor General-never pretended for one moment that the legislation before this committee was based on the statute of 1914. In fact, that statute was not mentioned by any hon. gentleman who took part in the discussion until after my hon. friend from South Renfrew had referred to it, and had based an argument in his speech upon it. The Government's action in this regard has excited widespread public interest. It has been referred to at publio meetings, and it has been discussed in the press all over Canada. Only this morning the Ottawa Citizen, in a leading editorial, after alluding to an article that had appeared in the Government organ in this city, took up this phase of the matter and said:
The Ottawa organ does not, for example, devote one word to a discussion of section 24 of the statutes, under which the Government guaranteed 45 million dollars' worth of the bonds of the company In 1914. This section is the crux of the whole matter; it is under that clause that the country is entitled to take over the system without the expenditure of an extra .dollar of the taxpayers' money. The matter is dismissed with a display of partisan rhetoric. Says our contemporary:
"The opposition arguments in parliament have been quite variegated. Hon. Mr. Pugsley contends that the Government should confiscate the road. He claims that the Government made provision for that when a Government loan to the road was made in 1914. Maybe so; but if the present plan is better, why object to it? And the Liberal parliamentarians in 1914 proclaimed that the present plan is better. They demanded it. TTiey advocated purchase of the company's stock by arbitration, with a limit price of $30,000,000. But now Mr. Pugsley demands confiscation.
The Citizen proceeds:
"If the present plan is better, why object to it?*' The present plan, briefly, provides for the arbitration of a matter which is not open to arbitration, and exposes the country to financial damages of very extensive range. We may be compelled to pay any sum the board of arbitrators decides we should pay, between 60 million dollars and one dollar. In any event, we are bound to be mulcted.
Of course the tu quoque argument must be introduced; it has proved such a valuable weapon in all matters wherein the administration have failed to bring forward reasonable arguments in support of their various measures since their advent to power. But our contemporary suppresses the facts...
And this part of the editorial I would commend to my hon. friend from Vancouver.
But our contemporary suppresses ' the facts when it merely states that the Liberals advo cated arbitration of the Canadian Northern stock several years ago, with a limit price of 30 millions. The Liberal proposition in amend-

ment to the Government's proposal to give the Canadian Northern the amount asked (45 million dollars) in 1914, was that the stock issue of the company should be reduced from 77 millions (instead of being allowed to stand at 100 millions as the administration proposed) to 30 millions, and that all of this stock should be placed in the hands of a trustee, for the benefit and security of the people of Canada, and that it should remain there five years, so that, in the event of default the Government would have power to take possession of the road without the expenditure of a single extra dollar. In the event of the road carrying on its operations and paying its way for five years, the country was to have the right to take over the stock by arbitration, provided it was thought desirable by Parliament that such a step should be taken. This is such an entirely different thing from the meaning intended to be conveyed by the bare statement that the Liberals proposed arbitration with a (limit price, in 1914, of 30 million dollars, as to lead to the conclusion that it is made by our contemporary either in ignorance or with a desire to distort the facts.
Instead, however, of accepting that amendment, which was proposed by Hon. Mr. Pugsley, the Government proceeded to draw up the agreement with the railways which is now under discussion. The chief jewel of this agreement was the clause which the administration is now discrediting. The task of protecting the interests of the country on this occasion was entrusted to the solicitor-general, and it was under the skilful direction of this minister that the famous clause was drawn up. Of it, at the time, the Minister of Finance said that he was lost in wonder-wonder that in one mortal could be compressed the wisdom and foresight to evolve a legal safeguard which could be so readily evoked on behalf of the people of the Dominion as that embodied in clause 24. Sir Thomas White said that he wanted to take off his hat to the solicitor-general for his wonderful ability and great ingenuity in this allimportant matter. To-day, however, the Minister of Finance is not lost in "wonder, love and praise," as the old hymn has it, but rather he is busy showing that the masterpiece of 1914 is in reality merely a legal frill, of no value in the agreement, and that it can be disregarded without in any way affecting the business in hand, which is to pay out an unknown sum of the money of the taxpayers to certain clever and accomplished railway contractors and promoters who have no legal claim to it.
In an attempt to discredit tihe Drayton-Acworth Commission and to give a value to the Canadian Northern railway stock which it does not possess, the Government has alleged that this commission, of their own creation, and headed by the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, omitted to take into account certain matters which should have been taken into account. In connection with this statement by the Government there is one very strange and very significant feature. It is a strange and significant thing that the Government has not asked the commis-

sion whether it did or did not make the alleged omissions, and it it did make the omissions what explanation it has to otter for having done so. That would be the natural and the courteous thing to do. Instead of doing this, however, the Government simply ignores the commission. The Minister of Finance stated in reply to an inquiry of mine in the House a few weeks ago, that the Government had made no application for information on that point. The Government chooses to ignore the commission and instead of going to the commission for an explanation of this alleged omission it goes to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. What is obtained from the company? The information obtained is set out in a letter of the financial comptroller of the Department of Railways and Canals, which was read in this House by the Minister of Finance on the 23rd of the present month, and which will be found on page 5139 of Hanr sard. I have not the slightest doubt in the world that the financial comptroller of the Department of Railways and Canals set out in this letter exactly what the company told him, and the criticism I have to offer regarding the contents of this letter applies altogether to the statement of the railway company and not at all to the financial comptroller of the Department of Railways and Canals.

In conclusion, I submit that the only terms upon which the people of Canada will approve the taking over the Canadian Northern system will be:
1.	The payment only of what the Canadian Northern may, upon proper investigation, be proved to be worth.
2.	The complete elimination from the management, control and operation of the road of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann and Messrs? Walker and Lash.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has, among other things, traced, to his own satisfaction at least, the genesis of this transaction, which, by the way, is the first step to be made by the Parliament of Canada in the nationalization of railways. He has traced the genesis back to 1911, when,-he says, eighteen Liberals of Toronto signed a manifesto against the Reciprocity agreement, and he finds, to his own satisfaction again, that these Liberals were all connected with the group to which the Canadian Bank of Commerce and the National Trust Company belong. I wish to point out to my hon. friend (Mr. Murphy) that he could not find in the city of Toronto more representative men than those who signed that manifesto in 1911. They were not of any one group at all. Let me point out to my hon. friend the names of those who signed that manifesto. There was Mr. John L. Blaikie, one of the most respected citizens of Toronto, president of the Canada Landed and National Investment Company. He was not connected with the group to which my hon. friend referred. Then there was Mr. W. D. Matthews, ex-president of the Toronto Board of Trade and vice-president of the Dominion Bank, of which Sir Edmund Osier is president. Then, Mr. W. K. George, ex-president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and of the Toronto Industrial Exhibition, and vice-president of the Sterling Bank of Canada; Mr. Somers, vice-president of the Board of Trade and president of the Sterling Bank *of Canada. Mr. R. S. Gourlay, president of the Toronto Board of Trade, and a piano manufacturer; the late Sir W Mortimer Clark, LL.D., ex-Lieutenant *Governor of Ontario, one of the most respected citizens not only of Toronto

and of Ontario, but of the whole Dominion; Mr. R. J. Christie, president of Christie, Brown & Company, and a prominent manufacturer-Mr. Christie is on the board of the Dominion Bank; Hugh Blain, of Eby, Blain & Company, leading wholesale merchant and director not of any bank, but of the Globe, the chief Ontario organ of the Liberal party; Mr. H. S. Strathy, director and for many years general manager of the Traders Bank of Canada; Mr. Goldman, managing director of the North American Life Assurance Company-not in any way connected with the group to which my hon. friends refers-Mr. J. A. Somerville, who held the same position in the Manufacturers Life Insurance Company-both well known insurance men; Wellington Francis, a prominent lawyer and director of the Standard Bank and of several companies in Toronto; Mr. J. D. Allan, ex-President of the Board of Trade; Mr. John C. Eaton, now Sir John Eaton, president of the T. Eaton Company, Limited, said to have 17,000 employees in his service. Sir John Eaton is one of the best known commercial men in Canada;	-though I am
not positive-that^\?8^>ri the board of the Dominion Bank. My hon. '*friend, therefore, is rather far-fetched m his argument when he traces the genesis, as he says, of this important transaction to the manifesto signed by eighteen citizens of Toronto with respect to reciprocity in 1911.
My hon. friend has said a good deal about the Bank of Commerce. I have before me a list of the directors of the Canadian Bank of Commerce and of its committees throughout Canada. I find that amongst the directors throughout Canada there are eighteen Liberals and nine Conservatives.
I find among the leading directors of the Canadian Bank of Commerce Hon. W. C. Edwards, a most intimate friend of the leader of the Opposition. I find that at the time the list was published the late Hon. Bir Lyman Melvin Jones was a member of the Board of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. He was reputed to be the closest intimate friend in Toronto of the leader of the Opposition. I find also the name of Mr. F. P. Jones, general manager of the Canada Cement Company, a strong Liberal; and of Mr. H. C. Cox, son of the late SenatorCox, one of the pillars of Liberalism, and one of the greatest personal friends of the leader of the Opposition. In addition to that, among the members of the Sherbrooke Committee of the bank I find the name of F. N. Mc-Crea, Esq., M.P., our respected colleague in this House. Tbe only reason I bring this

forward is to show that my hon. friend is somewhat far-fetched in his argument with regard to the political affiliations of the bank.
He has stated that the National Trust Company has obtained some Government business since 1911. I may point out to my hon. friend that trust companies which hold trust mortgages on railway enterprises to secure bond issues are usually named by the railway company subject to the approval of the Government. The very first trust mortgage that was executed by the Canadian Northern Railway Company to secure Government guaranteed bonds was executed during the regime of the Government of which my hon. friend was a member through the same National Trust Company. There is nothing strange, or unusual, therefore, in the National Trust Company being appointed trustee under the mortgage securing guaranteed bonds.
The hon. gentleman in the House the other night referred to Mackenzie, Mann & Company as the masters of the Administration. I have always understood that Sir Donald Mann was one of the pillars of the Liberal party. When Sir Donald comes to Ottawa, it looks like the scene of a great Liberal convention; most of my friends opposite are at the Chateau or at the club to do him reverence. We had better see things in their true light.
My hon. friend is trying to make out that a group prominently associated with the Conservative party are responsible for this legislation. Let me tell him that if he wants to get back to the real genesis of the railway situation that confronts us to-day and has confronted us for six years, he must go back to the railway policy of the late Administration. We are confronted, as I have pointed out, not with a theory but with a condition. I have pointed out where the responsibility lies for the railway policy ' which has produced the result that we have been discussing here for the last couple of weeks.	The genesis of it
was the guarantee of $35,000,000 on the line of the Canadian Northern between Montreal and Port Arthur. The genesis was the policy of connecting the Canadian Northern with the shores of the Pacific, as recited in the preamble to that Act under which $35,000,000 were guaranteed by the late Government in 1911. This Government has had to face and deal with a railway situation. Notwithstanding what my honourable friend may say about groups, the situation is simply this: the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern
systems will go into liquidation unless assisted by the Government. It is not a matter of groups at all. This is too large a situation to be dealt with, if I may say so without disrespect, in the petty partisan spirit in which it has been dealt with in this House and in this debate. Honourable gentlemen should not put forward arguments that they have put forward with regard to this situation; it is too large, too important.
My honourable friend has referred to the Drayton-Acworth report; he has said that the Government is seeking to discredit it. On the contrary, I stated that' it was an admirable report. Moreover, the Government's railway policy follows the main lines of the Drayton-Acworth report, so far as we can follow it to-day. The Drayton-Acworth report recommended the taking over of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Grand Trunk. We are not going so far as that at this time, but we are taking over the Canadian Northern in precisely the way that Sir Henry Drayton and Mr. Ac-worth recommended, at least so far as taking the stock instead of taking the physical assets of the road is concerned. In their report on this matter Messrs. Drayton and Acworth recommended the creation of a Dominion Railway Board. I quote from their report, page LVIII:
In order to give the Board of Trustees-
That is, the Dominion Railway Board, which they recommended should be formed.
-control of the railways mentioned, the following stock should be tranferred to them:
Canadian Northern.-The $40,000,000 common stock vested in the Canadian Government should be assigned by the Government to the trustees, and also (subject to, what we report below as to compensation for existing equities) the $60,000,000 still remaining in the hands of private persons.
The Drayton-Acworth report did not recommend that the Dominion Railway Board should take action under the legislation of 1914, although the Commissioners suggest that if the Canadian Northern would not transfer this stock, subject to certain consideration of their equity, the legislation of 1914 might be used as a club to make them do so. But what they suggested was that the $60,000,000 of stock of the Canadian Northern outstanding in the hands of private persons, should be transferred to the Dominion Railway Board! just as we are providing now that it shall be transferred to the Dominion Government. They do not suggest that we should foreclose under the legislation of 1914. We are

following the lines of the report so far as we can consistently with a programme which we are adopting, namely, the taking over first of the Canadian Northern Railway system. Although I do not emphasize the point because it has been referred to over and over again in the course of this debate, there is no doubt that there has been an omission of assets. The financial comptroller of railways has taken the matter up himself in the audit of the books, and he has drawn it to the attention of both Professor Swain and Sir Henry Drayton. There is no doubt that the land grants and the deferred payments on land sales were omitted with the cash and accounts receivable. Professor Swain, on page 43 of bis report, points out specifically that cash on hand is a physical asset. He also mentions the working capital, and he says:
Your attention is called to these two matters for the reason that neither have been included in the present valuation, and it may be desirable for you to inquire as to the cash on hand and to take account of it as well as of a proper allowance for working capital, in whatever use you may wish to make of the results of this valuation.
We are therefore adopting the mode prescribed by the Drayton-Acworth report, namely, of acquiring the stock rather than the physical assets of the system, and without doubt they were right in that mode because, as I have repeatedly pointed out in this House, it lends itself to the financing of the railway company.
My hon. friend (Mr. Murphy) has referred to a number of articles from newspapers of good standing, but I will point out to him that it is not possible for the Government to trace down all statements made in newspapers. We would not make very much headway with legislation in this House if we busied ourselves with taking up all statements made by newspapers, even those of high standing, throughout the Dominion, in relation to such legislation. My hon. friend read an article from the Montreal Star in which it stated that certain assets were omitted. I have no knowledge of such assets being omitted. In order that the House and the country may know that the Government has fairly accurate information with respect to this transaction,
I desire to say this: That the following investigations into the affairs of the Canadian Northern Railway Company have been made by this Government:
1. In respect of all lines subsidized, the expenditure has been checked both by the engineers of the Department of Railways and Canals and by the Government auditors. 
2.	In 1914, the Government appointed three auditors to investigate the finances of the company. A complete survey was made from the inception of the company down to the beginning of 1914. All receipts and expenditures of the company were investigated, and a complete report of the Government auditors has been tabled in the House.
3.	The legislation of 1914 called for the filing by the company of a condensed balance sheet of the whole system properly audited. This has been done. Since that date the engineers and the auditing staff of the Department of Railways and Canals have been keeping in touch with the construction going on on the system and investigating the expenditures in connection therewith.
4.	The legislation of 1916 provided for the appointment of independent Government auditors. We appointed one of the leading firms of .auditors, a firm of international reputation and standing, Messrs. Marwick, Mitchell, Peat and Company, well-known,
I have no doubt, to all the members of the House. They have audited all the books of the company for the Government.
5.	In addition to that under the legislation of 1916, we appointed a Royal Commission to investigate the affairs of the Canadian _ Northern Railway Company. This commission made a very complete report which has been under discussion in this House.
In addition to that, the directors of the Canadian Northern Railway Company appointed a board of New York experts to investigate the affairs of the company. That,
I believe, was made public.
_ We have, therefore, had very full information as to this, and I may say to my hon. friend that, so far as I know, there is no mystery in connection with the affairs of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. We have had their affairs under continuous investigation by the Railway Department, and we are not aware of any assets that have been omitted, nor are we aware of any disclosures which will be made such as my hon. friend has suggested.
I believe that this transaction carried out will result in the Dominion of Canada acquiring a great railway system which will, for the present and in the future, inure to the benefit of the people of Canada. The present position is that we are a shareholder to the extent of 40 per cent. All that we are doing is acquiring the majority interest, and we are acquiring it in a manner that would be considered fair as between

man and man. If the stock has no value, the arbitrators will so find; if it has some value, the arbitrators will so find. Why should we assume that the arbitrators will find a value that does not exist? We have given an earnest of our intention in the matter by appointing the Chief Justice of Ontario as one of the arbitrators. Unless the Chief Justice of Ontario agrees to the award as to the value of the stock, there is an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. Why should we not have confidence in our own courts? What reason have we to assume that the Supreme Court will deal with this matter otherwise than they deal with other matters, that is to say, fairly,
[DOT] judicially and impartially? What reason have hon. gentlemen opposite to suggest that any hut a fair result will come from this arbitration?	*
My hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy), at the outset of his remarks, asked for a good deal of information, most of which has been laid upon the table of the House. He asked in regard to the Montreal Tunnel and Terminal Company as to damages. I laid upon the table of the House a statement by the solicitor of the company, a gentleman in whom I have every confidence, and I have been assured, since my hon. friend made his remarks respecting claims for damages, that that report deals with all claims of which the railway company has notice, save for this, that in some cases, the matter is to stand for a year. A tunnel is not an unusual thing in Tailway construction. Take the tunnels in New York. The experience has been that the damages are not very considerable by reason of the construction of those tunnels. My hon. friend has referred to many claims for damages of which he has heard.

speechtext:
With Tegard to other claims, how far would that matter advance the discussion of this measure? This is a big transaction, a transaction in which we are acquiring the control of a railway system. Any claims for damages in connection with the Montreal Tunnel and Terminal Company will have to be dealt with in the usual way. If they are sound claims, they will he an obligation of the Tunnel ahd Terminal Company. The situation is not changed in respect to those by what we are doing. My hon. friend would not suggest that, in the taking over of a great railway system, the fact that there were some outstanding claims should stand in the way of a transaction of that magnitude. My hon. friend raised another question this afternoon. He said, are there long standing contracts between the company and its officials?
I am officially informed that there are no %uch outstanding long-date contracts. I am told there are only two contracts entered into, and those were in connection with operating men, and were cancelled some time ago.
I have given nractically all the information that my hon. friend has asked for. He also raised the question in reference to which the Prime Minister replied by telegram to the Prime Minister of British Columbia respecting the Canadian Northern. I have obtained a statement in regard to that. I do not believe it will advance the discussion of this matter very much, but still I have such regard for this House that I try to get all information that is asked for. The statement is as follows:

C.N.P. 41% Securities Guaranteed, $10,000,000. As to 1, the Main Line has been completed. The first 100 miles on the Island have been fully graded, but not railed on account of the impossibility of obtaining steel. So far as item No. 1 is concerned, there are practically no further obligations to be assumed with the exception of tracklaying on Vancouver Island Line.
As to 2 (a), the construction of the line between New Westminster and Vancouver has been deferred. In the meantime the company has entered into a running rights arrangement with the Vancouver, Victoria & Eastern railway to use their line between these points. This arrangement had the sanction of the local authorities, the line being opened for traffic by them accordingly. In view of the fact that this avoids duplication of lines and will answer the purposes of traffic for many years, it may be expedient to subsequently consider making this arrangement permanent.
As to 2 (b)-New Westminster to Steveston Line graded and track laid. Connection with Main Line at New Westminster end, including bridge over North Arm of the Fraser River yet to be constructed, this portion being deferred pending consideration of utilization of existing lines of another railway.
As to 2 (c), Victoria-Union Bay Lirie is coi.pleied and in operation.
As to 2 (d)-Vancouver Island Extension. Line graded to Alberni. Construction north of this point deferred owing to war.
As to 2 (e)-Kamloops to Vernon. Branch line from main line into city of Kamloops under construction and certain rights-of-way acquired. Construction on balance of line deferred owing to war.
As to 3-Terminals. The company's programme for terminals at Pacific Coast points involved an expenditure of approximately $10.000,000, of which the principal works were in the City of Vancouver. It was intended that these facilities would be provided from time to time to meet the requirements of traffic upon the opening of the various lines- The warhaving begun prior to the completion of any of the lines, this delayed the company's terminal programme. Contracts, however, were made with various parties for the necessary, filling of False Creek and the construction of a station, terminal, freight sheds, etc. This work is in progress at the present time and it is expected will be completed ready for operation early in the New Tear. The agreement 
with the Province of British Columbia does not specify the extent of the obligation of the company in respect to these terminals, it being merely provided that the proceeds of the guaranteed securities above mentioned should be entirely expended for such purposes.
It should be noted that the original contract with the province made under date of 2nd April, 1910, has been modified in certain particulars by special arrangements between the company and the province, and it is specifically provided in the contract that if, owing to unforeseen engineering difficulties or other circumstances beyond the reasonable control of the company, it will be impossible or impracticable to carry out absolutely the terms of the agreement, the Lieutenant-Governor may from time to time authorize amendments therein so long as the spirit of the agreement is not departed from.
With respect to the construction of the balance of the mileage referred to in 2, conditions arising out of the war have rendered it impossible at the present time to proceed with the further construction of branch lines. No change in these conditions can be expected until at least some time after the conclusion of the war, and even then unforeseen circumstances may arise which will require an entire readjustment of the arrangement between the company and the province with respect thereto.
Municipal Obligations.
The Canadian Northern Pacific railway has not entered into any contract with any municipality in British Columbia with the exception of the City of Vancouver, with regard to the False Creek terminals. Considerable progress has been made in the performance of this contract and the work is still under way, provision for this being largely included under the terminal securities guaranteed by the province. Owing to conditions arising out of the war, this work, in common with the work upon the lines of railway, has been more or less delayed, but the contract with the municipality makes provision for extension of time due to delays arising by reason of strikes.
That is the answer to my hon. friend with respect to the British Columbia situation. I think, I have covered most of the points he referred to, except what he stated in closing. My own view is that the Canadian Northern Railway Board will have to be constituted by the Government, of men of high standing, who will administer the affairs of that company in an absolutely efficient and non-partisan manner. The present board will have to be changed. The Government will have to constitute the board of the Canadian Northerii railway, when it becomes a government organization, in such fashion as to get the best results, not only from an operating standpoint, but also from the standpoint of the public interest. It is manifestly impossible for me to say how the board will be reconstituted, but it must be changed; there is no question in my mind about that.

As far as the operating staff is concerned, it would be a misfortune-I think my hon. friend will agree-if the railway company should lose the services of its skilled operating staff. That question to my mind should not arise. Looking to the future, and adopting, as I have said, the principles of the Drayton-Acworth report, one can see the operating board, appointed by the Dominion Government in some such fashion as has been recommended in the Drayton-Acworth report, administering the Canadian Government Railway system throug'iout Canada. That is what one would look forward to seeing, and I believe the people of this country will support a policy looking to that end in connection with the acquisition and operation of such railway systems as may come into the hands of the Government of Canada.
I am sorry my hon. friend looking at this great transaction, which, as I stated, is the first step towards railway nationalization in Canada, sees only the secondary and subsidiary features of it. The fundamental issue in the transaction which is now before the House is that the Government of Canada is acquiring a great railway system. It is the beginning of public ownership of Canadian railways; I do not say of all Canadian railways, but it is a great step forward. That is the main and fundamental fact. The question of purchasing the $60,000,000 stock owned by the majority shareholders is really a secondary and subsidiary question.

The transaction is, of course, an important transaction, but unless hon. gentlemen on both aides of this House are going to be here all summer we must make progress with this Bill.
